q: Does the paper's local-correction integral (Section 3, singularity of the free-space Green's function handled analytically over one leaf box) actually yield the O(h^{2k+2}) convergence one would naively expect for degree-k polynomial cell fits, or only the observed empirical O(h^{2k}) reported in Table 2?
basis: Our uniform-grid point-source baseline (C3) drops relative L2 error by only about 2x per doubling of N_side (32->64->96->128 gives 0.50 -> 0.14 -> 0.07 -> 0.04). This is essentially O(h) because the log-kernel singularity dominates. The paper achieves E2 ~ 4.9e-6 at N=96,592 with the 4th-order adaptive scheme, which is ~10^4 better than our baseline at similar N. All of that improvement must come from the local correction integral, but the paper does not explicitly report a convergence sweep for JUST that piece.
next_steps: Implement the paper's local correction integral in isolation on a single leaf box with a known polynomial source, and sweep k = 4, 6, 8 vs h. Verify the slope of log(error) vs log(h) matches the theoretical rate. If it exceeds the paper's reported per-example numbers, then the paper's global error is dominated by tree-refinement heuristics rather than the local correction, which would suggest tighter refinement criteria could improve accuracy at fixed N.

q: How much of the paper's claimed asymptotic O(N) FMM cost depends on the hierarchical M2M/L2L upward/downward passes versus a flat single-level M2L (like the one we implemented)?
basis: Our pure-Python FMM uses only the leaf-level M2L (each pair of well-separated leaf boxes translated independently) and shows per-target work scaling as O(N_boxes), which puts the whole solve at O(N sqrt(N)) rather than O(N). Timings in Table C2: T(8000) = 10.86s vs T(4000) = 0.67s (16x slowdown for 2x N). Yet even hierarchical FMMs (Greengard 1988) have a break-even N below which the flat approach is faster because of the M2M/L2L constant. The paper does not report where its own break-even falls.
next_steps: Add hierarchical M2M and L2L passes to our fmm2d.py, then rerun C2 with N up to 10^6 (needs uicgpu). Plot T vs N in log-log for flat, hierarchical, and direct; extract crossover N and asymptotic slopes. Contrast with the paper's implicit rate (Table 2, ~1e5 pts/s at N=8e5).

q: For the three-Gaussian problem (Example 4.1), how does the paper's adaptive quadtree behave as alpha grows from 250 to 10^4 or 10^5 -- do we hit the paper's 10-level cap before the requested FMM tolerance is achieved?
basis: The paper only reports alpha=250, which gives Gaussian widths sigma = 1/sqrt(2 alpha) ~ 0.045, comfortably resolved by ~10-level refinement (~ 2^-10 = 1e-3 finest cell). But PIC-plasma and medical-imaging applications routinely have alpha ~ 10^4-10^6, giving sigma ~ 1e-3 to 1e-4 -- below the paper's finest cell. Our experiments only ran alpha=250; we don't know where the algorithm silently degrades.
next_steps: Re-run the paper's Example 4.1 machinery (once P2 is implemented) with alpha in {250, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5} on the same requested tolerances (RHS 1e-9, FMM 1e-9). Record leaf count, max level attained, actual E2/Einf achieved. Identify the failure mode (level cap hit, E2 saturates, T explodes).

q: In the paper's periodic case (Table 4), the FMM must be augmented with an Ewald sum for the doubly-periodic Green's function. The paper devotes only ~1 paragraph to this. At what N does the augmented-FMM actually beat a periodic 2D FFT solver (naive O(N log N))?
basis: Our C4 (FFT/DST on Dirichlet) hit rate 1.2e7 pts/s at N=4M on modern hardware. The paper's FMM in Table 4 quotes ~1e5 pts/s (2001 hardware). Even scaling by 55x for modern hardware, the FMM would land at ~5.5e6 pts/s -- still 2x slower than plain FFT on regular grids. The FMM's win therefore must come entirely from adaptivity. The break-even point is not reported in the paper.
next_steps: Build a periodic-FMM (Ewald-augmented) and compare against a plain FFT solver on the same three-Gaussian problem, once at uniform 128^2 (FFT-dominant regime) and once at ADAPTIVE 128^2-equivalent with 90% of nodes in 4 small clusters (FMM-dominant regime). Plot break-even fraction of adaptivity.

q: Does the paper's stated 4th/6th/8th-order convergence in h persist when the RHS f has jump discontinuities (piecewise-constant f rather than smooth Gaussians)?
basis: The paper's Example 4.1 uses smooth Gaussians (infinitely differentiable), Example 4.2 solves Laplace equation with a boundary singularity but zero RHS, and Example 4.3 is again smooth. No experiment stresses the interior of f with a discontinuity. But real applications (interface flow, phase-field models, X-ray tomography) commonly have piecewise-constant or piecewise-smooth source terms. Convergence of a polynomial-in-cell fit to a discontinuous f collapses at the interface unless refinement is targeted at the discontinuity.
next_steps: Set up a test where f = 1 inside a smooth-boundary shape (e.g. offset ellipse) and 0 outside; the exact solution is a Newtonian potential integrable via a boundary integral. Run the paper's adaptive scheme at nominal order 4, 6, 8 vs h and check whether refinement to the interface recovers 4th/6th/8th order or falls to 1st (as a naive polynomial cell fit would predict).
